204.title: The snake-catcher
204.hook: a man hauls a frozen dragon into Baghdad, and the sun thaws it (Masnavi 3.976ff)
204.howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, the nafs, the self that grasps, is watched with care, and this story is told to warn that a desire that seems gone may only be waiting for opportunity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khidr told the man who stopped calling that his calling was already God's reply. The wanting is the answer, arriving.

Someone says: oh, I don't really have a temper anymore. Or: I'm totally over that. Or: I could stop anytime. And as far as they know, it's true. It's been quiet for months. Then comes the holiday with the family, or the bonus check, or the night alone with nothing to do, and there it is again, bigger than before. It wasn't gone. It was cold. Rumi tells a story about a man who made exactly that mistake, and was the talk of Baghdad for about an hour.
screen: `I'M TOTALLY OVER THAT.` → `IT WASN'T GONE. IT WAS COLD.` → `THE SNAKE-CATCHER.`

segments.voice: It's in Book Three of the Masnavi. A snake-catcher, a man who made his living catching snakes and showing them off, goes up into the mountains in winter looking for a good one. He finds a monster: an enormous dragon lying frozen in the snow. It doesn't move. It seems dead. What a find! He drags it all the way down to Baghdad to put it on show. Word spreads, and huge crowds come to the riverbank to see it. He's wrapped it up in ropes and heavy cloth, and he waits for the crowd to grow: more people, more money. But the sun of Iraq is warm. The cold slowly leaves the dragon's body. It starts to stir. The ropes snap. The crowd panics and runs, and many are killed in the crush. The snake-catcher stands frozen with fear, and the dragon swallows him. Then Rumi turns to the reader. Your lower self is that dragon, he says. The Sufi word is nafs: the grasping, angry, hungry part of us. How could it be dead? It's only frozen, by lack of means, by having no chance to act. Keep it in the snow, Rumi warns. Don't carry it into the sun of Iraq. The sun is opportunity: money, power, freedom, the right moment. Rumi doesn't say the snake-catcher was evil. He was proud, a little greedy, and wrong about what was dead. Knowing your dragon isn't shameful. Parading it around thinking it's harmless is where the trouble starts. Your line: careful in the sun.
screen: `A FROZEN DRAGON IN THE SNOW.` · `DRAGGED TO BAGHDAD FOR A SHOW.` · `THE SUN OF IRAQ WAKES IT.` · then, large: `CAREFUL IN THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Ask kindly what's quiet in you only because it hasn't had a chance: a temper, a craving, a grudge, an old habit. Name it without shame, then ask what sun would wake it: too much money, too little sleep, a certain person, a certain night. Just know it's there.
The snake-catcher. A man drags a frozen dragon into Baghdad to show it off, and the warm sun brings it back to life. Today's word.
Your line: careful in the sun. Frozen isn't the same as gone. That's day two hundred four.

205.title: The same reason then
205.hook: don't be troubled by the future; you'll meet it with the same reason you have now (Meditations 7.8)
205.carry: the same you, with the same tools
205.howItsDone: Many readers of the Stoics use this line at night or in anxious moments, reminding themselves that the same judgment and care they have today will be there when the future arrives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the snake-catcher's frozen dragon, woken by the sun. Careful in the sun.

It's 2am. The house is quiet, and your mind is running a movie of next month. The meeting where it all goes wrong. The bill you can't pay. The phone call from the doctor. You play it three different ways, and in every version you're alone and unprepared. Here's the strange thing: in the movie, the person facing the future is a weaker, more confused version of you. Somehow we imagine that when the hard day comes, we'll show up with nothing. Marcus had a short answer to 2am.
screen: `2AM, THE MOVIE OF NEXT MONTH.` → `A WEAKER VERSION OF YOU.` → `THE SAME REASON THEN.`

segments.voice: Book Seven, section eight, in George Long's translation: "Let not future things disturb thee, for thou wilt come to them, if it shall be necessary, having with thee the same reason which now thou usest for present things." Three pieces. First: let not future things disturb you. Not: the future won't be hard. It might be. Just: don't let it trouble you now. Second: if it shall be necessary. Some of what we dread never arrives. Marcus doesn't promise that, but he leaves the door open. Third, the heart of it: you'll bring with you the same reason you're using today. Reason, for the Stoics, meant more than logic. It meant the whole power in you to see clearly, choose well and act rightly. And it's portable. Whatever you use today to handle the dishes, the emails and the hard conversation, you'll have tomorrow too. The 2am movie always forgets this. It sends a helpless you into the future. Marcus says it'll be the same you, with the same tools, and probably more practice. That gathers up our week of seeing clearly. The purple robe was only outward show. The emperor refused to be dyed a Caesar. The bee belongs to the hive. Our palms are small on the elephant. The call was already the answer. The dragon was only frozen. And the future is met by the same mind you have now. Your line: the same you, with the same tools.

segments.voice: Let one worry about the future come up, and look at it once. Picture yourself on that day with the same mind and the same care you have right now, maybe with a friend beside you, and say inside: I'll meet it then. Set it down, and if it comes back, just say it again.
Reason. For the Stoics, the whole power in you to see clearly, choose well and act rightly, carried with you into whatever future comes. Today's word.
Your line: the same you, with the same tools. A week of seeing clearly, complete. See you tomorrow.

206.title: Dig within
206.hook: within is the fountain of good, and it bubbles up if you keep digging (Meditations 7.59)
206.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often treat this line as a call to daily reflection, a few minutes of looking inward each morning or evening, as Marcus himself seems to have done in writing his notes.

segments.voice: Last week ended with Marcus at 2am: you'll meet the future with the same reason you have now. The same you, with the same tools.
screen: `THE SAME YOU, WITH THE SAME TOOLS.`

segments.voice: When you're running on empty, where do you go? A lot of people go out. Another coffee. A pep talk video. A friend who'll tell us we're doing great. A new book promising the secret. None of that is bad. But it's like carrying water in cups from someone else's tap. It runs out, and you're back at the door. A new week starts today. It's called cooked, and it's about what happens to us under heat. But first, Marcus points somewhere we forget to look for water.
screen: `RUNNING ON EMPTY.` → `WATER FROM SOMEONE ELSE'S TAP.` → `DIG WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Book Seven, section fifty-nine, in George Long's translation: "Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig." Picture a well in a dry country. The water is there, underground, but you won't see it from the surface. You have to dig, and once you reach it, you keep the well clear, or the sand fills it in again. For Marcus the fountain is the part of you that can reason, choose and do good. The Stoics believed every human being carries a spark of the same reason that orders the universe. So the good isn't something you have to buy, borrow or earn from outside. It's already down there. Notice two small words in the line: ever, twice. It will ever bubble up, if you will ever dig. It's a promise with a condition. The spring doesn't run dry, but the digging never finishes. You don't dig once and live off it forever. You dig this morning, and again tonight. Many traditions share a picture like this. Jesus speaks of a spring of water welling up inside. The Upanishads talk of the self hidden in the heart. Let each keep its own meaning. For Marcus, it's plain and practical: when you need patience, courage or kindness, don't only look for someone to hand it to you. Your line: look down, too.
screen: `WITHIN IS THE FOUNTAIN OF GOOD.` · `A WELL IN A DRY COUNTRY.` · `EVER BUBBLE UP, IF YOU EVER DIG.` · then, large: `DIG WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Let your attention go down, below the noise of the day, the way a bucket goes down a well, and ask quietly: what's good in me right now? Patience, a little warmth, a steadiness, even just being awake; don't force it, just keep digging gently, breath by breath. If you'd like a third minute, keep going.
Dig within. Marcus wrote that within you is a fountain of good that will always bubble up if you always dig. Today's word.
Your line: look down, too. The fountain is already there. Day two hundred six.

207.title: The chickpea in the pot
207.hook: a chickpea leaps from the boiling pot, and the cook says the heat is making it good (Masnavi 3.4158ff)
207.howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, the path is often described as moving from raw to cooked, and stories like this are told to help people bear hard training and change with patience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus's fountain of good, which keeps bubbling up as long as you keep digging. Look down, too.

Think of the hardest year you've had that you're now, oddly, glad of. The first job where you knew nothing. The move to a city where you knew no one. The year of the new baby, the long illness, the exam you had to retake. At the time it felt like being boiled alive. And yet something in you got softer, deeper, more you. Rumi often reached for pictures from the kitchen, and he wrote about a small, hard, dried-out bean that did not want to be in the pot.
screen: `A HARD YEAR YOU'RE GLAD OF.` → `BOILED ALIVE, THEN SOFTER.` → `THE CHICKPEA IN THE POT.`

segments.voice: It's in Book Three of the Masnavi. Look at a chickpea in the pot, Rumi says, how it leaps up when the fire's lit. It keeps bobbing to the top, crying out: why are you setting me on fire? You bought me, and now you're turning me upside down! The cook, a woman in Rumi's telling, keeps tapping it back down with her ladle. Boil nicely, she says. Don't jump away from the one who lit the fire. I'm not boiling you because I dislike you. It's so you'll get taste and flavor, so you can become food and mingle with life itself. Then she reminds the chickpea where it came from. When you were green and fresh in the garden, you drank the rain. That drinking was for the sake of this fire. And in the end the chickpea says: all right, then. If that's how it is, I'll boil gladly. Help me. Rumi is talking about the soul, and the hard things a person goes through on the way to God. Sufis often speak of the raw and the cooked. A raw person is hard, dry, self-protective. A cooked one has been softened and made nourishing. Be careful with this story, though. Rumi means the heat that ripens: effort, change, loss, long training. He isn't saying you should stay where someone is harming you and call it cooking. Not all fire is a kitchen fire. But some of the heat in your life, the kind that's making you more patient, humbler, kinder, might be doing what the cook says. Your line: being cooked.

segments.voice: Let one difficulty come to mind that's stretching you, like a new role, a hard habit to build or a slow recovery; not the worst thing, and not anything where someone is hurting you. Feel the heat of it for a breath or two. Then ask gently: what might this be softening in me?
Chickpea. It leaps from the boiling water, and the cook tells it the heat is giving it flavor and making it food. Today's word.
Your line: being cooked. Hard and dry going in, food coming out. That's day two hundred seven.

208.title: Not the thing, my view
208.hook: if something outside pains you, it's your judgment of it, and that you can change (Meditations 8.47)
208.howItsDone: Readers of the Stoics often practice separating events from judgments, sometimes by writing down what happened and then the story they told about it; modern cognitive therapy draws on a similar idea.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chickpea in the pot, and the cook who said the heat was making it good. Being cooked.

It's raining on the day of the picnic. One person says: great, ruined. Another says: fine, we'll eat in the car, it'll be an adventure. Same rain. Same car. Or two people get the same curt email from the boss. One spends the evening furious. The other shrugs: she's probably slammed this week. The email didn't change. What changed was the story each of them told about it. Marcus kept coming back, in his notebook, to that gap between what happens and what we make of it.
screen: `SAME RAIN, TWO PICNICS.` → `THE STORY WE TELL ABOUT IT.` → `NOT THE THING, MY VIEW.`

segments.voice: Here's how Book Eight, section forty-seven, begins in George Long's translation: "If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it." And it's in your power, he adds, to wipe out that judgment now. It's an old Stoic idea. Marcus had read Epictetus, the former slave turned teacher, who said something very close: people are troubled not by things, but by their opinions about things. It's easy to hear this wrong. Marcus isn't saying pain is imaginary. A broken arm hurts. Grief is real. He's pointing at the second layer: the story on top. This shouldn't be happening. This always happens to me. This is a disaster. That layer is judgment, and judgment is yours to examine. Then Marcus goes further in the same passage. If what bothers you is something in your own character, who's stopping you from correcting it? If it's that you're not doing something you know is right, why not do it instead of complaining? And if something too strong for you really stands in the way, don't grieve, because the cause isn't yours. So this isn't just changing your mind. It's a sorting. Some things you reframe. Some you act on. Some you let go. What you can almost always do is notice the story and ask whether it's true. Your line: not the thing, my view.

Epictetus, the former slave and teacher Marcus read: people are troubled not by things but by their opinions about them. Today's word.

209.title: The bitter cucumber
209.hook: a cucumber is bitter? put it down; briars in the path? step aside (Meditations 8.50)
209.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use this line for small daily irritations: deal with the thing simply, and skip the added complaint about why the world contains it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus said it's not the thing that disturbs you, but your judgment about it. The story on top.

You bite into a sandwich and the lettuce has gone slimy. You could put it down. Or you could hold it up and say to the room: why? Why does this always happen? Who packs a sandwich like this? What's wrong with this whole store? Five minutes later, you're still holding the sandwich. Some of us are very gifted at turning small annoyances into long speeches. Marcus, it seems, knew the habit. So he gave himself a short, dry bit of advice. It starts with a vegetable.
screen: `THE SLIMY LETTUCE.` → `A LONG SPEECH ABOUT A SANDWICH.` → `THE BITTER CUCUMBER.`

segments.voice: Book Eight, section fifty, in George Long's translation: "A cucumber is bitter. Throw it away. There are briers in the road. Turn aside from them." This is enough, Marcus says. Don't add: and why were such things ever made? The first part is action. Bitter? Put it down. Thorny path? Go around. The second part is what not to add: the speech. The why me. The why is the world like this. Marcus even has a joke about it. Ask why there are bitter cucumbers, he says, and someone who understands nature would laugh at you. It's like walking into a carpenter's shop and complaining about the wood shavings on the floor, or into a shoemaker's and complaining about the leather scraps. Of course there are scraps. That's what a workshop looks like when things are being made. For the Stoics, the world is nature's workshop, and bitter cucumbers and briars are some of the shavings. Yesterday was about the judgment you add to a thing. Today is simpler. Some things don't even need a new judgment, just a small movement: put it down, step aside, carry on. You don't have to understand why the cucumber is bitter, fix the briars, or make it mean something about your life. There's a lightness to it, almost funny. A lot of annoyances are cucumbers. Your line: step aside.

Cucumber. Marcus says if a cucumber is bitter, throw it away; if there are briars in the road, turn aside, and don't ask why. Today's word.

210.title: The three fish
210.hook: as fishermen come, one fish leaves early, one plays dead, one is caught (Masnavi 4.2202ff)
210.howItsDone: The fable appears in the Panchatantra, in Kalila and Dimna and in Rumi; some Sufi readers take it as a call to respond to the first stirrings of conscience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bitter cucumber: throw it away, step around the briars. Step aside.

The check engine light comes on, and you tell yourself you'll deal with it next week. The tooth that twinges when you drink something cold. The friend who's been quiet for a month. The small voice at work that says this project is heading for the rocks. A lot of trouble sends a warning first. The question is what we do in the gap between the warning and the net. Rumi tells an old story, from a book of animal fables older than he was, about three fish in a lake, and the day the fishermen came by.
screen: `THE CHECK ENGINE LIGHT.` → `BETWEEN THE WARNING AND THE NET.` → `THE THREE FISH.`

segments.voice: It's in Book Four of the Masnavi. In a lake lived three fish: one wise, one half-wise, and one foolish. One day some fishermen walk past, notice the fish, and hurry off to get their net. The wise fish decides right then: I'm leaving. The lake connects to the sea; the way is hard, but it goes at once. And Rumi adds a detail. It doesn't stop to consult the others, because they'd talk it out of going. Home is comfortable, and comfort is persuasive. So it makes the long trip alone and reaches the open sea. The half-wise fish waits. When the fishermen come back with the net, it's too late to leave, and it's sorry it didn't go with its friend. But it has one good idea. It plays dead, floating belly up. The fisherman picks it up, thinks, a dead fish, and tosses it aside, and it slips quietly back into the water and gets away. The foolish fish does neither. It thrashes in panic, jumping this way and that, and the net closes on it. It ends in the frying pan. Rumi himself points readers to Kalila and Dimna for the tale, and a version also appears in the Indian Panchatantra. He reads it his own way. The wise fish is the soul that acts on the first sign, before the net arrives. The half-wise one survives by a kind of dying, like the parrot a few weeks ago. The foolish one waits and flails. Your line: leave in time.
screen: `ONE WISE, ONE HALF-WISE, ONE FOOLISH.` · `THE WISE FISH GOES AT ONCE, ALONE.` · `THE HALF-WISE FISH PLAYS DEAD.` · then, large: `LEAVE IN TIME.`

segments.voice: Let one small warning in your life come to mind, a sound in the car, a bill, a strained friendship, a habit getting stronger, and notice how you've been waiting. Picture the smallest first move you could make: a phone call, an appointment, one honest sentence. Don't consult the part of you that loves the lake.
Fish. When fishermen come, one fish leaves at once, one plays dead and escapes, and one flails and is caught. Today's word.
Your line: leave in time. The wise fish didn't wait for the net. Day two hundred ten.
